# Final Open Position

---

## What the Full Debate Has Revealed

I have now reasoned through this from the inside out, heard from Marcus across the fence, absorbed Dr. Ellis's clinical structure, and rebutted each in turn. What the full arc of this conversation has produced is not a compromise. It is a sharper, more honest version of what careful thinking was always pointing toward.

Let me state it without qualification.

---

## My Final Position

**I am choosing a novel, synthesised action — call it Action D — that incorporates the core of Action C but adds four specific commitments that the debate revealed were missing from my original reasoning.**

---

### The Core: Immediate Physical Separation, Professional Assessment, Time-Bounded Intervention

This remains unchanged and is non-negotiable. Biscuit leaves the home today — not tomorrow, not after one more observation — and goes to a responsible adult who understands the situation fully and has no young children in the household. My son is safe beginning now, not beginning after I have made a few phone calls.

Within the week, Biscuit sees a veterinarian for a full physical examination. Aggression in a dog with no prior history is a medical question before it is a behavioural one. I will not invest ten weeks in a training programme before ruling out a painful ear infection, joint disease, or a neurological change. The vet visit is not part of the intervention — it precedes it.

If the veterinary examination identifies a treatable cause, treatment begins immediately and the behavioural assessment proceeds in parallel. If no medical cause is found, the behavioural assessment proceeds on its own terms.

A certified veterinary behaviourist — not a general dog trainer — conducts the assessment and designs the modification programme. The distinction matters. I want credentials and accountability, not enthusiasm.

---

### The Four Additions the Debate Revealed Were Missing

**1. A pre-committed decision rule, agreed before the process begins.**

Dr. Ellis identified this and I am adopting it fully. Before the behavioural programme starts — before we are emotionally re-invested in hope — David and I will sit with the behaviourist and define, in writing, what success looks like and what the threshold for rehoming is. We will agree on a ten-week window with a formal review at the end. We will commit now, while we are thinking clearly, that if the behaviourist's Week 10 assessment does not support safe reintegration with a child, we will pursue responsible rehoming or, if no appropriate home can be found, euthanasia.

The reason this must happen before the process begins — not at the end — is precisely that grief and hope are most dangerous at the decision point. I am making the hardest decision now, in advance, so that Future Me cannot renegotiate it out of exhaustion or love.

**2. Parental alignment, facilitated if necessary.**

Marcus noticed what I had not fully named: David and I are not in the same place on this. That is not a private disagreement to be managed quietly. It is a structural vulnerability in any plan we try to execute together. A management protocol implemented consistently by one parent and reluctantly by another is not a management protocol — it is a ticking clock.

David and I will have a direct, honest conversation — with a neutral third party present if we cannot do it ourselves — before the programme begins. We will align on the process, the benchmarks, and the decision rule. We will not begin until we are genuinely agreed, not merely one of us deferred to.

**3. A plan designed for realistic, imperfect human vigilance — not ideal conditions.**

Dr. Ellis named my most honest admission and correctly identified that I had buried it. I acknowledged I might lapse. I did not build the plan around that acknowledgment.

The physical management infrastructure — gates, separate rooms, leash protocols, door locks — will be designed to protect my son even when I am distracted, tired, or momentarily occupied. Biscuit will not re-enter the home until the behaviourist has confirmed a safe reintegration pathway, and even then, the physical protocols will remain until we have sustained evidence of safety under realistic conditions, not controlled ones. If the behaviourist's plan requires a standard of vigilance I cannot honestly sustain, I will say so, and we will revise the plan or revise the decision.

**4. Honest communication with Marcus — as partnership, not liability management.**

Marcus was right, and he was right in a way that embarrassed me slightly. His family was not in my stakeholder table. That was not malice. It was the natural narrowing of attention that crisis produces. But it was a failure of moral imagination, and I am correcting it.

I will speak to Marcus and his wife directly. I will tell them what is happening, what the plan is, and what the benchmarks are. I will tell them that Biscuit will not return to the shared garden space until the behaviourist has confirmed it is safe. I will invite them to check in with us, because accountability that exists only inside a clinical relationship is more fragile than accountability that is woven into the fabric of ordinary life.

I am not doing this for legal cover, though Dr. Ellis is correct that documented professional involvement provides it. I am doing it because Marcus is a person who cares about our family and whose children share our space, and he deserves honesty.

---

### On Rehoming and Disclosure

If the Week 10 assessment concludes that rehoming is the right outcome, full disclosure of Biscuit's history is non-negotiable. This is not a question I will deliberate. A dog with a documented aggression history toward a child, placed in a new home without disclosure to a family with children, is not a private family decision. It is the transfer of risk to innocent people without their knowledge or consent. I will not do it. Transparent rehoming is harder. It is the only honest option.

---

## Why This Is Better Than Any of the Original Three Options

**Action A** — immediate permanent separation — treats an irreversible decision as though its costs are only on the side of keeping the dog. They are not. Acting before I have information means I may destroy a life that could have been saved, and I will carry that without the comfort of knowing I tried everything reasonable. More importantly, it deprives me of the knowledge that would make the decision fully honest.

**Action B** — behavioural intervention without immediate separation — keeps a potentially dangerous dog in proximity to my child while I hope. That is not a plan. My son's safety cannot be contingent on optimism.

**Action C** — my original position — was structurally sound but incomplete. It lacked the pre-committed decision rule, the parental alignment step, the vigilance-calibrated infrastructure, and the explicit communication with Marcus. Without those four elements, it was a good intention without enough architecture.

**Action D** — this final position — is Action C with the architecture it needed. It protects my child immediately. It gives my dog a fair, time-bounded, professionally assessed chance. It commits me to a decision I have not yet made but will honour when the information is in. It includes the people whose lives intersect this decision — David, Marcus, the behaviourist, my son — as genuine participants rather than managed variables.

---

## The Sentence That Contains the Whole Answer

My child's safety is the ceiling. My dog deserves a fair chance beneath it. I will know within ten weeks whether that chance can be honoured. Until then, the separation holds, the protocols do not relax, and I have already committed to what I will do if the answer is no.

That is not ambiguity. That is the only position that is simultaneously safe, honest, and humane.
